I've been thinking lately about that exhausting feeling when you try to force yourself to focus on something your mind just doesn't want to engage with. Huberman mentioned how people with ADHD can have hyperfocus for things they're passionate about, but struggle with everything else. That hit something in me I wasn't expecting. It's not that we can't focus at all. It's that focus only comes naturally when our heart actually wants to be present.Something I read recently in What the Silence Tried to Say by Alira Sennel reminded me that maybe the problem isn't with us, but with how we try to force attention where our soul doesn't want to go. The book didn't try to fix me or give me techniques. It just whispered that there's a difference between what we think we should be doing and what our nature actually craves. Maybe focus can't be trained as much as it can be listened to.

I have noticed that one thing that doesn't get spoken about often enough is how the ADHD brain isn't always just inntattentive or distractible simply because it lacks the ability to focus.. but at times it can have difficulty weeding out all of the stimulus around it and is hyperaware to every sound, sight, smell, emotion, etc.. in you become overwhelmed by all of the inputs. The ADHD brain can be a very loud place. In my personal experience I can often have what feels like several thoughts at once and that makes it very hard to zone in on the one thing you are supposed to be paying attention to. This can also cause overwhelm that makes you feel hypersensitivie. On one hand I think people with ADHD have this insane knack for noticing things because they cannot help it. On one hand you can be very forgetful and spacey.. on the other hand you can sense every single thing every you and it can be triggering. I think some of these symptoms I am describing show up more often in women based on my research - Also I think this can show up in some ways that feel a little OCD. For example, when you become a high functioning person with ADHD and you hack your life.. for example you ritualize certain habits.. I always place my keys in the same exact place when I come in so that I can leave my house at the last possible moment and not have to search for my keys.. however let's say somebody moves my keys or moves my things.. even though it may seem disorganized to others it can completely disrupt my patterns or the learned behavious I have acquired for tracking my rhythms or how to move through my day and I can be supremely impatient with others. Really makes sense in the "method to the madness" .. anyhow, these are just my ramblings

Focus isn't something you manufacture—it’s something you return to. In the silence beneath the noise, awareness is always focused. ADHD, distractions, scattered thoughts—they’re surface ripples. But the ocean beneath is still. You are not the chaos. You are the space in which it happens. The more you identify with the swirl, the more focus feels like a fight. But when you rest as the witness, focus isn’t about forcing attention—it’s about remembering you were never separate from it.

The world doesn’t make this easy. It's built to fragment you—notifications, deadlines, constant stimuli all scream for your energy. But infinite intelligence isn't in a rush. It doesn't multitask. It moves in perfect rhythm, one thing at a time. You don’t need to “fix” your brain—you need to realign with the stillness behind it. Whether labeled ADHD or not, every being has access to the same field of pure presence. That’s the birthplace of real attention—not the kind that strains, but the kind that listens.

Improving focus, then, is less about doing more and more about being less. Less distracted by judgment. Less entangled in expectation. Less glued to the storyline. The more you root yourself in pure awareness, the more your mind learns to settle like dust in still air. Not because you forced it—but because you finally stopped chasing. The moment you are presence, focus happens on its own. It’s not effort—it’s home.

Something most people with focus issues never consider is how they are breathing. When you breathe through your mouth or overbreathe (which most people do without realizing it), you blow off too much CO2. Low CO2 causes blood vessels to constrict, including the ones feeding your prefrontal cortex. The Bohr Effect shows that hemoglobin holds onto oxygen more tightly when CO2 is low, so even with full lungs your brain gets less oxygen delivery. A Stanford experiment found that just ten days of forced mouthbreathing increased blood pressure by 13 points and destroyed sleep quality. Now imagine years of habitual mouthbreathing and what that does to sustained attention. I work with people on breath retraining and the ones who switch to nasal breathing and reduce their breathing volume consistently report better focus within weeks. Not because breathing is a magic fix but because their brain is finally getting proper blood flow and oxygen delivery. Normal breathing volume at rest is 4 to 6 liters per minute. Most stressed or anxious people breathe 10 to 15 liters. That gap is where a lot of concentration problems live.
